title: The Yi King
dateDisplay: Text c. 1000–800 BCE; appendixes c. 5th–3rd centuries BCE
attributionNote: The lineal figures and their judgements are older than Confucius, who is credited by tradition with the appendixes but certainly did not write all of them; the text and the treatises that explain it were formed over centuries and are printed together here.
description: The Yi King is the classic of change: sixty-four hexagrams built from broken and unbroken lines, each with its judgement and the texts of its individual lines, followed by the appendixes that read the figures as a cosmology of heaven, earth and man. Confucians studied it as a book of wisdom and of divination at once, and Legge's translation prints the text with the treatises that were ascribed to Confucius.
historicalContext: The book escaped the Qin book-burning as a work of divination and was read in the Han through the commentaries of the school of images and numbers; Wang Bi's third-century reading made it a philosophical text again. Legge translated it, with Prolegomena on its history and subject matter, for the Sacred Books of the East, volume 16 (1882).
availabilityNote: The text and the appendixes as Legge prints them: the sixty-four hexagrams and the treatises on the trigrams, the sequence of the hexagrams and the appended explanations, streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one printed section per chapter. Legge's prolegomena, the printed plates and the errata are volume apparatus and are not part of the work.
